title: How to lend and spend money to increase the gains from international migration
gist: McKenzie reports that of $40bn in World Bank migration/refugee-related lending in 2014-24 ($15bn migration components), almost all went to coping with refugee influxes, and only $110m across 7 projects (~0.015% of annual lending) supported labor mobility, despite migration being the highest-return known intervention. He surveys scalable options (TVET linked to foreign certification, national facilitation drives like Kenya's 1m/yr target, post-departure support) and notes philanthropy lacks proven, scalable migration vehicles.

insights.claim: Even relatively small increases in global migration could yield gains exceeding total foreign aid or the gains from removing all remaining trade barriers.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Labor mobility is a vastly underpriced development lever relative to aid and trade liberalization.
insights.quote: even relatively small increases in global migration could result in gains that far exceed the total of all foreign aid or the total gains from relaxing all remaining trade barriers

insights.claim: Migrants typically experience large, immediate and persistent income gains greater than any other evaluated policy intervention the author knows of.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Remittance flows and migrant income are structurally strong drivers of EM household income.

insights.claim: The author suggests countries could treat international migration as an industry to specialize in, using emigration and immigration strategically to build skills and new sectors.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Labor export as explicit industrial strategy could reshape remittance-dependent economies.

themes.theme: World Bank lending skewed to refugees

insights.claim: Between 2014 and 2024 the World Bank had 160 projects related to international migration and refugees totaling $40 billion, of which $15 billion went to migration components, about 5% and 2% of total lending respectively.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Sizes multilateral flows to migration-affected countries.
insights.locator: World Bank Lending on Migration and Refugees

insights.claim: Half of World Bank migration-related spending went to just eight countries: Uganda, Lebanon, Jordan, Turkey, Cameroon, Bangladesh, Colombia and Djibouti, almost entirely for coping with refugee influxes.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Refugee-hosting is a meaningful concessional-finance channel for these sovereigns.
insights.quote: half of all spending was just in the eight countries Uganda, Lebanon, Jordan, Turkey, Cameroon, Bangladesh, Colombia, and Djibouti
insights.locator: World Bank Lending on Migration and Refugees

insights.claim: Only $110 million across 7 projects in 2014-24, about $11 million a year or 0.015% of annual World Bank lending, aimed to increase international worker mobility or prepare workers for work abroad.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Labor mobility is almost entirely unfunded by multilaterals, a gap that could shift.
insights.quote: only $110 million across 7 projects, or approximately $11 million a year over 2014-24, (0.015% of the World Bank’s annual lending)
insights.locator: World Bank Lending on Migration and Refugees

insights.claim: Of 87 World Bank projects explicitly mentioning migration in their development objective, 80 address refugee influxes while only 7 have labor mobility as a high-level component (0.2% of projects).
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Institutional bias toward reactive refugee spending over proactive mobility.
insights.locator: Another way of understanding the focus

insights.claim: Global Skills Partnership pilots remain small proofs of concept, such as taking 105 Moroccans to Germany for tourism and hospitality apprenticeships.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Skills-partnership channels are not yet at investable scale.
insights.locator: Where are the opportunities to do more?

insights.claim: The key open question is how to effectively spend tens of millions on migration, an amount large enough to attract country directors and finance ministers, given very few evidence-backed scalable solutions.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Absence of scalable models is the bottleneck, not lack of returns.
insights.quote: We have very few evidence-backed scalable solutions
insights.locator: Where are the opportunities to do more?

insights.claim: Redirecting existing TVET spending toward foreign skill and certification requirements, as in projects in Bangladesh, Nepal, Papua New Guinea and Tonga, lets workers credibly signal skills to overseas employers.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Certification portability is the key unlock for labor-export programs.
insights.quote: workers not only need to gain the skills needed for international jobs, but they need to be able to credibly signal that they have these skills to overseas employers

insights.claim: Several African countries have set ambitious labor-export targets: Kenya aims to send 1 million workers abroad a year, Ethiopia 700,000, and Tanzania aims to sign agreements with eight destination countries.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Rising East African labor exports could lift remittance inflows and FX reserves over time.
insights.quote: Kenya aims to send 1 million workers abroad each year, Ethiopia 700,000

insights.claim: A $32 million World Bank loan to Papua New Guinea explicitly aims to strengthen government systems helping workers benefit from overseas employment, focused on Australia and New Zealand.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Rare example of multilateral lending directly for labor export.

insights.claim: Policy should go beyond social protection for migrants abroad to help them build skills, connect to home-country jobs and investment, and match into jobs on return.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Return-migration and diaspora investment channels are underdeveloped.

insights.claim: Despite enormous potential gains, few charities have proven solutions for using donations to expand migration job opportunities; Malengo has promising RCT evidence but only just over 300 students in Germany.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Migration-focused impact investing remains sub-scale and unproven.
insights.quote: there are few charities with proven solutions for using donations to expand migration job opportunities

insights.claim: The new Africa Jobs Fund backs ventures in export manufacturing and international labor mobility, including organizations placing African workers in Italy and Germany.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Emerging private/impact capital interest in labor-mobility businesses.

insights.claim: The author is not yet sure where a funder could productively invest $100 million in migration.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Even a leading expert sees no ready scalable vehicle; early-stage space.
insights.quote: I’m not sure yet where to tell a funder to invest $100 million in migration
